Q22923830.title: 2020 United States presidential election
paras: The 2020 US presidential election, held on 3 November 2020, set the Democratic ticket of former vice president Joe Biden and Senator Kamala Harris of California against the Republican incumbents, President Donald Trump and Vice President Mike Pence. Harris was the first African American and first Asian American to be nominated for vice president by a major party. The Libertarian Jo Jorgensen and the Green Howie Hawkins also ran.

The campaign was dominated by the COVID-19 pandemic and its economic effects, the protests after the police killing of George Floyd, the Supreme Court seat filled by Amy Coney Barrett after Ruth Bader Ginsburg's death, and the future of the Affordable Care Act. Because of the pandemic a record number of people voted early or by post: the Council on Foreign Relations counts about 65.6 million mail ballots and over 100 million early votes. Counting the mail ballots took days in some swing states, and the major news organisations did not project Biden the winner until the morning of 7 November.

Biden won 306 electoral votes to Trump's 232, and about 51.3% of the popular vote to 46.8%. His more than 81 million votes were the most ever cast for a presidential candidate, and turnout, about two-thirds of eligible voters, was the highest since 1900. He took back Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, which Trump had narrowly won in 2016, and also won Arizona and Georgia. The race was closer than the national margin suggests: by the CFR's count a shift of under 43,000 votes in Arizona, Georgia and Wisconsin would have produced a 269–269 tie.

Trump refused to accept the result, claimed without evidence that it had been stolen by fraud, pressed state officials and lost a series of court cases. The electors voted on 14 December 2020. When Congress met on 6 January 2021 to count their votes, a crowd of his supporters stormed the Capitol and interrupted the session; the count was completed and the result certified in the early hours of 7 January. Trump was impeached for a second time over the attack. He was the first president to lose a re-election bid since George H. W. Bush in 1992.

Q101110072.title: 2024 United States presidential election
paras: The 2024 US presidential election, held on 5 November 2024, was won by the Republican ticket of former president Donald Trump and Senator JD Vance of Ohio over the Democratic ticket of Vice President Kamala Harris and Governor Tim Walz of Minnesota. Trump, who had lost to Joe Biden in 2020, was running for a second, non-consecutive term.

Biden first ran for re-election and easily won the Democratic primaries. After a debate against Trump in June 2024 that was widely seen as a poor performance, concern about his age and health grew and Democrats in Congress called on him to step aside. On 21 July he announced in a letter that he was leaving the race and endorsed Harris, who became the nominee on 5 August, the first since 1968 who had not run in the primaries. Trump had become the presumptive Republican nominee in March after beating Nikki Haley, Ron DeSantis and others; on 13 July he was wounded in the ear in an assassination attempt at a rally in Pennsylvania, and on 30 May a New York jury had found him guilty on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records, making him the first former president convicted of a crime.

Voters named the economy most often as their main concern, followed by immigration, the state of democracy and abortion. Trump campaigned for mass deportation of illegal immigrants, higher import tariffs and an 'America First' foreign policy, and repeated false claims that the 2020 election had been stolen.

Trump won 312 electoral votes to Harris's 226, carrying all seven main swing states, and won the popular vote with about 49.8% to 48.3%, the first Republican to do so since George W. Bush in 2004. Pew Research's study of verified voters found that his coalition was more racially and ethnically diverse than in 2016 or 2020: Harris won Hispanic voters by only 51% to 48%, after Biden's 61% to 36% in 2020. Congress counted the electoral votes on 6 January 2025 and Trump was inaugurated on 20 January.

Q58767.title: Trans-Siberian Railway
Q58767.place: Russian Empire (Moscow to Vladivostok, with a branch across Manchuria)
paras: The Trans-Siberian Railway was built by the Russian imperial government to tie European Russia to Siberia and the Pacific coast. Before it, Siberia had few roads; goods moved by river in the few ice-free months and by sledge in winter. Tsar Alexander III ordered the line in March 1891, and the heir to the throne, the future Nicholas II, inaugurated the work at Vladivostok that May. The finance minister Sergei Witte backed the project as a driver of economic development.

The line was laid in sections, worked on simultaneously, by tens of thousands of labourers (Wikipedia gives 62,000; EBSCO says convicts made up most of the workforce, and Chinese and Korean workers helped on the Amur section). To shorten the route, an 1896 treaty with China allowed Russia to build the Chinese Eastern Railway straight across Manchuria to Vladivostok; it opened in 1903, the year the map uses, giving a rail route from Europe to the Pacific. Lake Baikal remained a gap: trains were carried across by an icebreaking ferry built in Britain, and in winter rails were even laid on the frozen lake, until a line around its southern shore was finished.

The single-track line could carry too little to supply Russia's armies in Manchuria in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905, which contributed to Russia's defeat. Afterwards Russia built the Amur line through its own territory north of the Chinese border, completed in 1916; since then the railway has run entirely within Russia, about 9,289 km from Moscow to Vladivostok across eight time zones, the longest railway line in the world.

The railway carried millions of peasant settlers east: Wikipedia counts about four million arriving in Siberia in the peak years 1906–1914, and EBSCO says the government paid for the resettlement of more than one million between 1892 and 1914. It also became a military artery, used by the Czechoslovak Legion and the Allied intervention in the Russian Civil War, and in the Second World War to move Soviet troops and industry and to bring in Lend-Lease supplies through Vladivostok.

Q101534.title: February Revolution
paras: The February Revolution was the first of Russia's two revolutions of 1917. It took place mainly in the capital, Petrograd (St Petersburg), and set striking workers and, decisively, the soldiers of the city's garrison against the government of Tsar Nicholas II, who was away at army headquarters in Mogilev. It began on 23 February in the Julian calendar Russia then used, 8 March in the Western calendar, which is why it is sometimes called the March Revolution.

On International Women's Day, women textile workers walked out over bread shortages and drew other workers with them (Wikipedia says over 50,000 that day, the marxists.org timeline 128,000). Within two days the strike had grown to about 200,000 and then some 250,000 people. On 26 February troops fired on crowds, and a company of the Pavlovsky Regiment mutinied. On 27 February the Volynsky Regiment rose, killing an officer, and most of the garrison followed. That day the Duma formed a Provisional Committee and socialists set up the Petrograd Soviet. On 1 March the Soviet's Order No. 1 told soldiers to elect committees and obey the Soviet. On 2 March, his train stopped at Pskov, Nicholas abdicated; his brother Grand Duke Michael declined the throne, ending the rule of the Romanov dynasty.

Discontent had long been building: Russia had modernised its economy without reforming the autocracy, and the First World War brought heavy defeats, inflation, food shortages and scandals around the court. Wikipedia gives over 1,300 people killed in the revolution in Petrograd.

Power passed to a Provisional Government of Duma liberals under Prince Georgy Lvov, which shared authority uneasily with the Petrograd Soviet ('dual power'). Lenin returned from exile in April. The government kept Russia in the war; after the July Days Alexander Kerensky became its head, but it lost support and was overthrown by the Bolsheviks in the October Revolution, which led on to civil war and the Soviet Union.

Q124425.title: Iron Curtain
Q124425.place: Europe, from the Baltic to the Adriatic (speech at Fulton, Missouri)
paras: The 'Iron Curtain' was the dividing line across Europe between the Soviet Union and the states it controlled in the east and the Western countries, most later in NATO, from the end of the Second World War until 1989–1991. The phrase is dated to 5 March 1946, when Winston Churchill, who had lost office as British prime minister the previous July, gave a speech titled 'The Sinews of Peace' at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri. President Harry Truman, who had encouraged the visit, introduced him.

Churchill said that 'from Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent', leaving the capitals of Central and Eastern Europe under Moscow's growing control. He argued that the Soviet Union wanted the expansion of its power and doctrines rather than war, that it respected strength, and that Britain and the United States should stand together in what he called a 'special relationship'. He had used the image before, in a telegram to Truman on 12 May 1945, and the phrase was older still: Queen Elisabeth of Belgium is reported to have used it in 1914, and Joseph Goebbels in February 1945.

The speech was controversial. Many American newspapers criticised it for antagonising Moscow, and Stalin answered in Pravda that it was a call to war, comparing Churchill's talk of English-speaking unity to Nazi racial theory. Together with George Kennan's 'Long Telegram', written days earlier, it helped harden the Truman administration's stance towards the Soviet Union.

The division the phrase described became real over the next years. The Soviet Union turned Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia (after the 1948 coup), Romania, Bulgaria and East Germany into satellite states, barred them from Marshall Plan aid, and from about 1950 almost stopped emigration to the West; borders were sealed with fences, minefields and watchtowers, and the Berlin Wall followed in 1961. The curtain began to open on 27 June 1989, when the Austrian and Hungarian foreign ministers cut through the border fence; communist rule fell across Eastern Europe that year, Germany reunited in October 1990 and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

Q486124.title: Battle of Badr
Q486124.place: Badr, southwest of Medina, Hejaz (present-day Saudi Arabia)
paras: The Battle of Badr was fought in March 624 (17 Ramadan in the second year of the Islamic calendar) between the Muslims of Medina, led by the Prophet Muhammad, and an army of his own tribe, the Quraysh of Mecca, led by Amr ibn Hisham, known to Muslims as Abu Jahl. Wikipedia converts the date to 13 March, HistoryOfWar.org to 17 March. It was the first large battle between the two sides and opened years of war between them.

After their migration to Medina in 622 the Muslims raided Meccan trade caravans. In early 624 a large Quraysh caravan led by Abu Sufyan was returning from Syria, and Muhammad set out to intercept it with about 300 men (traditionally 313) and very few horses. Abu Sufyan learned of the plan, turned his caravan away towards the coast and escaped, but sent to Mecca for help, and a relief army that outnumbered the Muslims about three to one marched to Badr anyway. The Muslims took the wells nearest the Meccans and denied them water.

The battle opened with single combats between three champions from each side, in which Hamza and Ali won their duels for the Muslims. The Meccans then attacked, but the Muslims countered, broke their line and killed several Quraysh leaders, Abu Jahl and Umayya ibn Khalaf among them. Wikipedia gives about 70 Meccans killed and about 70 taken prisoner, most later ransomed, against 14 Muslim dead.

The victory, which the Quran recalls as won 'when you were vastly outnumbered', strengthened Muhammad's standing in Medina and brought outside tribes into alliance with him; Muslims came to see it as a sign of divine help. Abu Sufyan became the leading figure in Mecca, and the war went on with the Battle of Uhud. Nearly everything known about Badr comes from Islamic traditions and biographies of Muhammad written down later.

sources.title: Surah Ali 'Imran, verse 123 (tr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)

Q51648.title: East–West Schism
paras: The East–West Schism is the break in communion between the Latin Church of the West, led by the pope in Rome, and the Greek Orthodox churches of the East, led by the patriarchs with Constantinople foremost. It is conventionally dated to 1054, when legates of Pope Leo IX and Patriarch Michael I Cerularius of Constantinople excommunicated each other, though scholars have proposed other dates and the split grew over centuries.

The two halves of the Church had long drifted apart over doctrine, ritual and authority: the Western addition of the Filioque ('and the Son') to the Nicene Creed, whether the Eucharist should use leavened or unleavened bread, and above all the pope's claim to universal jurisdiction against the East's view of the patriarchs as a shared leadership. Political rivalry, from Charlemagne's coronation as emperor in 800 to Norman conquests in southern Italy, added to the strain.

In 1053 Cerularius closed the Latin churches in Constantinople, and Archbishop Leo of Ohrid, with his backing, attacked Western customs such as unleavened bread. Pope Leo IX sent a legation under Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida, with Frederick of Lorraine and Archbishop Peter of Amalfi. The talks failed, and on 16 July 1054 the legates laid a bull excommunicating Cerularius and his supporters on the altar of Hagia Sophia, then left for Rome. Cerularius and his synod answered with a sentence against the legates. Pope Leo had already died, which made the legates' authority doubtful, and both sentences were aimed at persons rather than at whole churches.

The breach was not seen as final at once, but it deepened, above all after crusaders sacked Constantinople in 1204; reunions agreed at the councils of Lyon (1274) and Florence (1439) did not last. On 7 December 1965 Pope Paul VI and Ecumenical Patriarch Athenagoras I declared in a joint statement that they regretted the events and 'commit these excommunications to oblivion', while noting that this did not end the differences between the churches, which remain out of full communion.

Q172991.title: Council of Trent
Q172991.place: Trent (Trento), Prince-Bishopric of Trent in the Holy Roman Empire; briefly Bologna (Papal States)
paras: The Council of Trent was the Catholic Church's answer to the Protestant Reformation, counted by Catholics as the nineteenth ecumenical council. It met in three periods between 13 December 1545 and 4 December 1563 in Trent, a city in the Holy Roman Empire just south of the Alps, under three popes: Paul III, who called it, Julius III and Pius IV. The Emperor Charles V pressed for it; Protestant princes refused to take part.

Soon after Luther's Ninety-five Theses of 1517, he and the German diets called for a free general council, but rivalry between France and the Emperor, papal fear of councils limiting papal power and the Turkish threat delayed it for a generation; an attempt to meet at Mantua in 1537 failed. When the council opened in Trent cathedral only a few dozen bishops attended (New Advent lists 4 archbishops and 21 bishops). In 1546–1547 it decreed that scripture and church tradition together are the source of faith, made the Latin Vulgate the authoritative Bible and set out Catholic teaching on original sin and on justification. In March 1547 an outbreak of disease in Trent led the council to move to Bologna, and the council stalled.

Julius III reopened it at Trent in May 1551; it defined the doctrine of the Eucharist, and envoys of some Protestant princes came under a safe-conduct, but no agreement was possible, and in April 1552 the war between Maurice of Saxony and the Emperor broke it up. Pius IV reconvened it in January 1562. The last period issued decrees on communion under both kinds, the sacrifice of the Mass, holy orders, marriage, saints, relics and images and indulgences, along with reforms of the clergy and religious orders. At the close the decrees were signed by 255 members according to Wikipedia, 215 according to the Catholic Encyclopedia.

Pius IV confirmed the decrees on 26 January 1564. The council fixed Catholic doctrine against Protestantism and became the centre of the Counter-Reformation; its effects reached the Church's liturgy and its censorship of books. No further ecumenical council met until the First Vatican Council of 1869–1870.

Q192769.title: American Revolution
Q192769.place: The Thirteen Colonies of British North America
paras: The American Revolution was the rebellion of thirteen of Britain's North American colonies that created the United States. On one side stood the colonial assemblies, then the Continental Congress and its Continental Army under George Washington, later joined by France and Spain; on the other the British Crown and Parliament, their army and navy, and the colonists who stayed loyal (Loyalists). The map dates it from 1765, the year of the Stamp Act, to 1783, the year of the peace.

Britain came out of the Seven Years' War in 1763 heavily in debt and set out to raise revenue in America. Parliament's Stamp Act of 1765, a tax on legal documents and printed paper, met riots, boycotts and a congress of nine colonies arguing that taxation without representation in Parliament violated their rights as Englishmen; it was repealed, but the Townshend duties of 1767 renewed the quarrel. British troops sent to Boston fired on a crowd in the Boston Massacre of 1770. When Parliament gave the East India Company a monopoly on tea, colonists threw its tea into Boston Harbor on 16 December 1773. Parliament answered with the Intolerable Acts, closing Boston's port and putting Massachusetts under direct control, and in September 1774 a First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia and called a colony-wide boycott.

Fighting began at Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775. The Second Continental Congress made Washington commander-in-chief, voted for independence on 2 July 1776 and adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July. After the British surrender at Saratoga in 1777, France signed a treaty of alliance with the United States on 6 February 1778, and Spain entered the war in June 1779. In 1781 a British army under General Cornwallis was trapped at Yorktown, Virginia, by American and French forces and surrendered, which led Britain to seek peace.

Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay negotiated the peace; preliminary articles were signed on 30 November 1782 and the Treaty of Paris on 3 September 1783. Britain recognised the independence of the United States, with territory reaching west to the Mississippi, and agreed to settlements on fishing rights, pre-war debts and Loyalist property. The states, first joined under the Articles of Confederation, later adopted a stronger federal Constitution, which took effect in 1789.

Britain ended the Seven Years' War (1763) heavily in debt and raised colonial revenue.
The 1765 Stamp Act taxed legal documents and paper goods; it met riots and boycotts, and delegates of nine colonies (Stamp Act Congress) protested taxation without representation; it was repealed.
The Stamp Act Congress argued that taxation without representation violated colonists' rights as Englishmen.
The Townshend Acts (1767) renewed resistance; British troops in Boston led to the Boston Massacre of 1770.
Parliament gave the East India Company a tea monopoly; on 16 December 1773 colonists threw tea into Boston Harbor.

Parliament passed the Intolerable Acts (1774), closing Boston's port and placing Massachusetts under direct control; the First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in September 1774 and adopted a boycott.
War began at Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775; Congress appointed Washington commander-in-chief in 1775, passed the Lee Resolution on 2 July 1776 and adopted the Declaration on 4 July 1776.
After the British surrender at Saratoga (1777) France signed the Treaty of Alliance on 6 February 1778; Spain entered the war on 21 June 1779.
In 1781 Cornwallis's army was captured at Yorktown by American and French forces, leading Britain to negotiate.
Franklin, Adams and Jay negotiated; preliminary articles were signed on 30 November 1782 and the Treaty of Paris on 3 September 1783.
Britain recognised US independence and boundaries (territory east of the Mississippi), with terms on fishing rights, debts and Loyalist property.
The states were joined under the Articles of Confederation; the Constitution took effect in 1789.

Q179250.title: French invasion of Russia
Q179250.place: Western Russia, from the Neman River to Moscow
paras: In 1812 Napoleon invaded the Russian Empire of Tsar Alexander I with a multinational Grande Armée of more than 450,000 men drawn from France and its allied and subject states. His aim was to force Russia back into the Continental System, his trade blockade of Britain, which Alexander had abandoned at the end of 1810. The Russian armies under Barclay de Tolly and Pyotr Bagration numbered about 180,000–220,000 at the start, and Mikhail Kutuzov took overall command in August.

The army began crossing the Neman River from the Duchy of Warsaw on 24 June (the McGill timeline gives 23 June). The Russians retreated rather than give battle, and Napoleon's long forced marches and failing supply lines cost him huge numbers of men to weather, disease, desertion and lack of supplies. He took Smolensk after fighting on 17–18 August, but the Russian armies escaped. On 7 September Kutuzov stood at Borodino, west of Moscow; the battle was one of the bloodiest of the age and the French took the field, but the Russian army survived. Napoleon entered an abandoned Moscow on 14 September, and fires burned much of the city over the next days.

Alexander would not negotiate. After about five weeks Napoleon left Moscow on 19 October and tried to march southwest, but after the battle of Maloyaroslavets on 24 October he turned back onto the devastated road he had come by. The first snow fell on 4 November, and cold and hunger destroyed much of what was left of the army. Between 26 and 29 November the remnant fought its way across the Berezina River, and on 5 December Napoleon left the army and hurried back to Paris.

Wikipedia estimates that the campaign cost around a million lives, soldiers and civilians, within six months, with Russian military losses nearly as large as the French. The disaster broke Napoleon's hold on Europe: on 30 December the Prussian general Yorck signed the Convention of Tauroggen, Prussia and then Austria changed sides, and the War of the Sixth Coalition followed.

Q199820.title: Paris Peace Conference
Q199820.place: Paris (Quai d'Orsay), with the German treaty signed at Versailles
paras: The Paris Peace Conference was the meeting at which the victorious Allies of the First World War settled the terms of peace for the defeated Central Powers: Germany, Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria and the Ottoman Empire. It opened on 18 January 1919 at the French foreign ministry on the Quai d'Orsay. Delegates of some thirty countries took part, but the decisions were made by the 'Big Four': Georges Clemenceau of France, David Lloyd George of Britain, Woodrow Wilson of the United States and Vittorio Orlando of Italy. The defeated states were given no voice in the talks, and Soviet Russia was not represented.

The Allies arrived with clashing aims. Wilson wanted a peace built on his Fourteen Points of 1918 and a League of Nations to keep it; France sought security against Germany and compensation; Italy pressed claims on the Adriatic that Wilson opposed. The League's Covenant was written into the treaties. Japan's proposal of 13 February 1919 to add a clause on racial equality won 11 of 17 votes but was ruled to need unanimity and failed. Germany's rights in Shandong were transferred to Japan rather than returned to China, which set off the May Fourth Movement in China and led China to refuse to sign.

The conference produced five treaties: Versailles with Germany (28 June 1919), Saint-Germain with Austria (10 September 1919), Neuilly with Bulgaria (27 November 1919), Trianon with Hungary (4 June 1920) and Sèvres with the Ottoman Empire (10 August 1920). By the Treaty of Versailles Germany accepted, in Article 231, responsibility for the war and liability for reparations, which were set in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks; it lost about a tenth of its European territory and all its colonies, and its army and navy were limited. German and Ottoman overseas possessions became League 'mandates', mostly under Britain and France.

Wikipedia dates the end of the conference to 21 January 1920, though the historian Michael Neiberg notes that the process did not really end until July 1923. The US Senate refused to ratify the Versailles treaty, falling seven votes short on 19 March 1920, so the United States never joined the League and made a separate peace with Germany in 1921. The treaties redrew the map of Europe and the Middle East, and the resentment they caused, above all in Germany, is widely seen as one of the roads to the Second World War. The Treaty of Sèvres was later replaced by the Treaty of Lausanne of 24 July 1923.

Q165058.title: Holodomor
Q165058.place: Soviet Ukraine (and the Kuban region of the North Caucasus)
paras: The Holodomor ('death by hunger' in Ukrainian) was the man-made famine of 1932–1933 in Soviet Ukraine, part of a wider famine in the grain-growing regions of the Soviet Union. It was caused by the policies of Joseph Stalin's government, which forced Ukraine's peasants into collective farms and then seized their grain; its victims were overwhelmingly Ukrainian villagers.

From late 1929 the regime collectivised agriculture by force and 'dekulakised' better-off farmers, whose property was confiscated and who were shot, imprisoned or deported. Harvests fell, but Ukraine was still set very high grain-delivery quotas. A law of 7 August 1932 made the taking of collective-farm grain, even gleaning ears from the fields, punishable by labour camp or death. In November 1932 the Ukrainian party, under Vyacheslav Molotov's direction, ordered villages and farms that failed their quotas to be blacklisted: they were cut off from trade and fined in meat and potatoes, and homes were searched for hidden grain. On 22 January 1933 a directive sealed the borders of Ukraine and the Kuban to stop starving peasants leaving to look for food.

Deaths peaked in the spring and early summer of 1933. The Encyclopedia of Ukraine cites demographers' estimate of just under four million deaths in Ukraine for 1932–1934, the best estimate to date, with about 3.5 million in the first half of 1933 alone; Wikipedia gives 3.5 to 5 million in recent scholarship and notes that higher figures have also been cited, such as the 7 to 10 million in a 2003 joint statement at the UN. The state rejected foreign relief, and the famine eased with the better harvest of 1933.

The Soviet Union denied the famine and banned discussion of it until the late 1980s. Historians agree that it was man-made, but disagree on whether it was deliberately aimed at Ukrainians: some argue that Stalin used starvation to crush Ukrainian resistance and national feeling, others that it was the result of collectivisation and forced industrialisation. Ukraine recognised the Holodomor as genocide in 2006, and Wikipedia counts more than 30 other UN member states and the European Parliament that have done the same.

Q154681.title: Anschluss
Q154681.place: Austria (Vienna, Linz and the German border)
paras: The Anschluss ('joining') was the annexation of Austria by Nazi Germany in March 1938. It set Adolf Hitler and the Austrian Nazis against the government of Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg, which tried to keep Austria independent but had lost the protection of Mussolini's Italy. Union with Germany had been popular in Austria after 1918, but the peace treaties of Saint-Germain and Versailles forbade it; in July 1934 Austrian Nazis had murdered Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss in a failed coup.

At Berchtesgaden on 12 February 1938 Hitler forced Schuschnigg, under threat and in the presence of German generals, to give the Austrian Nazi Arthur Seyss-Inquart control of the police and security and to amnesty jailed Nazis. On 9 March Schuschnigg called a referendum on Austrian independence for 13 March. Hitler answered on 11 March with an ultimatum: cancel the vote and resign, or Germany would invade. That evening Schuschnigg resigned in a radio address and told Austrians not to resist; Seyss-Inquart was made chancellor after midnight. German troops crossed the border early on 12 March without meeting armed resistance, and on 13 March a law declared Austria part of the German Reich. On 15 March Hitler spoke to a huge crowd on Vienna's Heldenplatz.

Repression began at once. Wikipedia reports about 70,000 arrests within days; the Gestapo hunted down Social Democrats, Communists and other opponents, and Schuschnigg was placed under arrest. Austria's roughly 200,000 Jews faced weeks of violence and humiliation, such as being forced to scrub the streets, and then all of Germany's anti-Jewish laws; many tried to emigrate. A plebiscite on 10 April 1938 reported about 99% approval, after 300,000 to 400,000 people, among them Jews, Roma and political opponents, had been barred from voting.

No foreign power intervened: Britain and France had largely accepted a union as inevitable, and the Anschluss became an early example of appeasement, followed in September 1938 by the Munich agreement on the Sudetenland.

Q150812.title: Invasion of Poland
paras: The invasion of Poland in September 1939, which began the Second World War in Europe, was a joint attack on the Polish Republic by Nazi Germany, with a small Slovak force, from the west, north and south, and by the Soviet Union from the east. A week earlier Germany and the Soviet Union had signed a non-aggression pact, the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, whose secret protocol divided Poland between them. Poland's allies Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September but gave it very little practical help.

To justify the attack, the SS staged a fake Polish assault on a German radio station at Gleiwitz on the night of 31 August, and Nazi propaganda claimed that Poland was persecuting its ethnic Germans. At dawn on 1 September German forces crossed the border: the USHMM counts nearly 1.5 million men, about 60 divisions and more than 2,000 tanks, with a large air force that destroyed most of Poland's roughly 300 aircraft in the first days. Poland, which had mobilised only part of its army of about a million men, could not hold its long borders. German troops reached the outskirts of Warsaw by 8–9 September, and the Polish defeat on the Bzura river in mid-September decided the campaign.

On 17 September the Red Army invaded eastern Poland, and the Polish government left the country for Romania. Warsaw surrendered on 28 September after heavy shelling and bombing, Germany and the Soviet Union fixed a new border between their zones at the end of September, and the last Polish units stopped fighting after the battle of Kock on 6 October. Wikipedia lists about 66,000 Polish soldiers killed and about 690,000 taken prisoner, against about 16,000 German and 1,500 Soviet dead.

Poland ceased to exist as a state. Germany annexed its western regions and Danzig on 8 October and placed the rest under a 'General Government'; the Soviet Union incorporated its share into its own republics. Germany's aim, in Wikipedia's words, was to end Poland as a sovereign country, with its citizens destined for extermination. Poles continued the war through an underground state at home and armed forces in the West under a government in exile.

Q129053.title: Partition of India
Q129053.place: British India, above all the Punjab and Bengal
paras: The partition of India in August 1947 divided British India into two independent dominions, India and Pakistan (whose eastern wing later became Bangladesh). It ended British rule and split the provinces of the Punjab and Bengal by district, according to whether Muslims or non-Muslims (mostly Hindus and Sikhs) were the majority. The main parties were the British government, represented in India by the viceroy Lord Mountbatten; the Indian National Congress; and the Muslim League, which since its Lahore Resolution of 1940 had demanded sovereign Muslim-majority states.

Communal tension had grown through the 1940s. After the British Cabinet Mission's plan for a loose federation failed in 1946, the Muslim League's 'Direct Action Day' on 16 August 1946 set off the Great Calcutta Killings, in which about 4,000 people died by official count. On 3 June 1947 Mountbatten announced a plan for partition and set independence for August; Indian leaders accepted it, and the British Parliament passed the Indian Independence Act on 18 July. In July Sir Cyril Radcliffe, a British lawyer who had never been to India, was given about five weeks to draw the new borders, using population figures and undefined 'other factors'. Pakistan came into being on 14 August and India became independent on 15 August 1947, but the Radcliffe Line was only published on 17 August.

The division set off one of the largest and most violent migrations in history. Some 12 to 20 million people crossed the new borders in both directions (the 1951 censuses of India and Pakistan counted about 7.3 and 7.2 million refugees), most in the Punjab, where Muslims fled west and Hindus and Sikhs east. Massacres killed between 200,000 and 2 million people; Wikipedia notes that most scholars accept a figure of about one million, and Al Jazeera puts it at more than one million. Tens of thousands of women were abducted on both sides.

Violence spread beyond the two provinces, to Jammu and Kashmir from September 1947, and partition reshaped the populations of the Punjab, Bengal and cities such as Delhi, which about 330,000 Muslims left and about 500,000 Hindu and Sikh refugees entered.

Q164348.title: Hungarian Revolution of 1956
Q164348.place: Budapest and the rest of Hungary
paras: The Hungarian Revolution of 23 October to early November 1956 was a nationwide uprising against Hungary's communist government and the Soviet domination behind it. On one side were students, workers, armed insurgents and, for a few days, a reforming communist government under Imre Nagy; on the other the State Protection Authority (ÁVH, the security police), hard-line communists, and the Soviet army, which crushed the revolt.

Under Mátyás Rákosi Hungary had been a Stalinist police state. After Stalin's death Nagy was prime minister from 1953 until Rákosi ousted him in 1955, and in 1956 Khrushchev's criticism of Stalin and concessions won by Poland encouraged hopes of change. On 22 October students drew up demands that included the withdrawal of Soviet troops, free multi-party elections and the removal of Stalin's statue in Budapest. On 23 October a mass demonstration followed; when a delegation tried to broadcast the demands from the radio building, the ÁVH fired on the crowd, and fighting spread. The party named Nagy prime minister and called in Soviet troops already in Hungary, but this first intervention was limited. Insurgents formed militias and freed political prisoners, workers' councils took over local government, and some communist officials and ÁVH men were killed. By the end of October fighting had largely stopped: Nagy's government disbanded the ÁVH on 28 October, on 30 October announced a return to a multi-party system, and on 1 November declared Hungary neutral and leaving the Warsaw Pact, informing the UN.

But Soviet troops were entering Hungary rather than leaving it. On 4 November Soviet forces attacked Budapest in strength, and János Kádár, who had left Budapest for the Soviet side, was put at the head of a new government. Nagy took refuge in the Yugoslav embassy. The last organised resistance ended around 10–11 November, though fighting went on in places after that. About 2,000–3,000 Hungarians and about 700 Soviet soldiers were killed. The United States and the UN protested but did not intervene, their attention divided by the Suez crisis at the same time.

More than 200,000 Hungarians fled abroad, most to Austria. Thousands were arrested and many deported to the Soviet Union. Nagy left the embassy on 22 November and was arrested; he was tried in secret and executed in 1958. Kádár stayed in power and later pursued a gradual reconciliation, including the economic reforms of 1968.
